Representatives from Canada Post and Tŝideldel First Nation celebrate the official opening of the Tŝideldel Post Office on Monday, Nov. 2. Chief Otis Guichon Sr. signs the ceremonial first letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, to be mailed from the newly opened Tŝideldel Post Office on Monday, Nov. 2. The ceremonial first letter from Chief Otis Guichon Sr. to Prime Minister Mark Carney, alongside Canada Post Truth and Reconciliation stamps. For decades, Tŝideldel residents travelled to neighbouring Chilanko Forks to collect mail addressed under another community’s name. Now, they have a post office at home, and a mailing address that reflects it. The Tŝideldel Post Office opened Nov. 2 at 710 Redstone Flats, following years of work by Tŝideldel Development Corporation and Canada Post to bring postal services into the community. Clayton Charleyboy, an elected Tŝideldel First Nation councillor and the executive director of Tŝideldel Development Corporation, said residents expressed pride that their mailing addresses will now identify their community rather than neighbouring Chilanko Forks. “So our identity was tied to somewhere we didn’t live,” he said. “We are in the Chilcotin, far away from major cities. We have been displaced a few times, and Tŝideldel is the last place we ended up, so Tŝideldel means home to me,” said Otis Guichon Sr., Nits’ilʔin (Chief) of Tŝideldel First Nation in the media release by Tŝideldel Development Corporation and Canada Post Beyond the name on the address, Charleyboy said the outlet gives residents access to mail in a secure, lit and maintained setting within their community. 59ca811dc5854047bba7ecb8aee38eda.text: Environment Canada is warning on Nov. 5, 2026 of moderate to strong gusty winds in the southern Interior. A special weather statement is warning of moderate to strong gusty winds for several regions in the Interior. According to the statement by Environment Canada on Thursday, Nov. 5, the winds are expected to start Thursday evening and last until Friday evening in the Cariboo, Prince George, 100 Mile House (including Highway 97) and South Thompson regions. The weather alert states it is for the south Cariboo including Williams Lake. “A strong low pressure system will approach the B.C. coast this evening and will bring a prolonged period of southeast winds with gusts ranging from 60-70 km/h to the B.C. interior,” the statement says. The southeast winds will pick up in the evening and are expected to peak by Friday morning. They may ease slightly on Friday afternoon before an incoming cold front is expected to bring a strong push of southwest winds, with gusts possibly up to 90 km/h between Quesnel and Prince George. Winds for the South Thompson region are expected to peak Friday afternoon, with the strongest winds expected near Cache Creek. A potentially stronger storm is set to follow on Saturday evening, Environment Canada says. “Local utility outages are possible. Parks and forests may sustain damage. Secure loose objects,” the statement reads. “Weather in the mountains can change suddenly resulting in hazardous driving conditions.” “Please continue to monitor alerts and forecasts issued by Environment Canada. To report severe weather, send an email to BCstorm@ec.gc.ca or post reports on social media using #BCStorm.”

a5c2f2a0d25f5420a0f14b0396f04d1e.text: The 2026 federal budget includes $6.5 billion to support the forestry industry. Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne unveiled the 2026 budget in Ottawa on Thursday, promising a slew of initiatives to help boost the economy amid trade uncertainty. Titled “Masters of Our Destiny,” the budget document is fully geared toward protecting Canadian economic sovereignty. It also keeps spending in the red for the foreseeable future. This budget projects a $62.3-billion deficit this fiscal year, which would grow slightly to $62.5 billion next year, then fall to $57.6 billion the year after. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre took to social media, calling it a “credit card budget” and saying it will cause Canada’s debt to soar and mean “higher taxes tomorrow.” The forestry sector is set to gain, with $6.5 billion earmarked for the industry over the next six years. This adds to the $2.9 billion announced to support forestry since August 2025. According to the budget, the new funding is to be spent on increasing fibre supply, modernizing forestry facilities, supporting higher-value product production and expanding market opportunities. Most of this money, $4 billion, is slated for a new Forestry Sector Accelerator to invest in large biorefineries, biofuel facilities and other “higher-value” forestry production. Kim Haakstad, president of the B.C. Council of Forest Industries, welcomed the finding, but said funding alone won’t save the sector. “We need a clear strategy with concrete actions and timelines to get more wood moving, attract investment and protect forestry jobs and communities,” she said in a written statement. The budget also seeks to boost support for western resource extraction by offering to sell a 15-per-cent stake in the Trans Mountain Corporation, owner of the TMX oil pipeline, to 128 individual Indigenous groups in B.C. and Alberta. Members of the white nationalist group Loyalist Pioneers were seen on the steps of the B.C. Legislature on Oct. 25, the morning following the 2026 provincial election. Victoria resident Julie Baetz was on her daily commute to work when she spotted a peculiar sight at the B.C. Legislature. A dozen people, all dressed in black and wearing masks, walked up the steps of the legislative building before unfurling a banner bearing the word “remigration” and the name Loyalist Pioneers. Watching from a distance, Baetz took a few pictures, and a quick online search confirmed her suspicion that the group was a white nationalist organization, making an appearance the day following the Oct. 24 provincial election, in which Conservatives won a sweeping majority. According to the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, the group is classified as part of the “white nationalism 3.0” or “Active Club” movement — an emerging decentralized network of alt-right groups using physical fitness, combat sports, and camaraderie to recruit members into white supremacist and extremist activities. Spreading across Canada over the past few years, the group is part of a broader movement that includes Second Sons and Nationalist-13, whose primary focus is anti-immigration. The word “remigration,” displayed on the group’s banner, is a modern political buzzword used by far-right movements to promote the mass deportation or forced expulsion of immigrants and their descendants. According to Edwin Hodge, an adjunct professor at the University of Victoria who specializes in extremism, radicalization and conspiratorial ideologies, the term is now considered a “white nationalist dog whistle.” “Their sort of narrative is that they simply want to help non-white folk return to their land of origin,” he said. “But if you read their internal messaging, violence is always a part of that equation.” Unlike the white nationalist movement of the

b2ac268cb152c6a4ae288c92468863ce.text: Panago was first started in Abbotsford in 1986, growing to 170 locations by 2026. Panago's head office is located in Abbotsford, which is where the pizza chain first started in 1986. What started as a small group of Abbotsford pizzerias in 1986 has since grown to approximately 170 locations all across Canada. Panago was first launched under the name Panagopoulos 2 for 1 Pizza Place by the Rooke family, who also created several other local businesses. After a number of name changes and expansions in the decade after opening, the company also added Sean DeGregorio to its team, who now serves as Panago’s CEO. Being involved from so early on in the company’s journey has been a special experience, said DeGregorio. He’s also particularly proud that what started as an Abbotsford company, and is still headquartered in the city, has been able to achieve such growth in just 40 years. “It was the people of Abbotsford who gave us a chance and kept coming back for pizza,” said DeGregorio. “We owe this community a lot.” Panago now employs nearly 3,000 people across its 170 locations, and sells more than six million pizzas per year. “I’m proud of our local owners and their teams,” said DeGregorio. “They’re the ones making the pizza and giving people a reason to come back, just like they did here.” As part of the pizza chain’s 40th birthday celebration, Panago has launched special promotions throughout November. Many locations will also host a Customer Appreciation Day event on Nov. 29 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. “Our 40th birthday is an opportunity to thank the customers, franchisees, and communities who have been part of Panago’s journey,” said DeGregorio. “We’re proud of how far we’ve come and excited to celebrate this milestone with the people who helped make it possible.”

Four Canadian Armed Forces members injured in the fire at CFB Wainwright have been transferred to health-care facilities in B.C. and Ontario. The transfers follow “careful medical assessment and recommendations from medical professionals,” according to the latest update from the Department of National Defence Wednesday (Nov. 4). The four were moved to be closer to their home communities where they can continue receiving the medical care they need, while being closer to family and loved ones, the update adds. Twenty-five people remain hospitalized, while 14 others have since been released from hospital. Four soldiers, Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, were killed. “Recovery will look different for each injured person and their family. Some may face a long journey ahead, but they will not face it alone,” the statement says. The Military Police has been tasked with an independent investigation into the fire. It’s being conducted independently of the Canadian Armed Forces chain of command, an Oct. 22 update said. A Board of Inquiry will also be conducted as a separate and independent process. The department says those are typically conducted following the completion of an investigation, but they could happen concurrently when doing so does not compromise the integrity of the investigative processes. The department says the boards of inquiry are led by the Canadian Armed Forces and they are fact-finding investigations “which will try to determine how an incident came about and whether any lessons can be learned from it to prevent recurrence.” On Oct. 17, a fire was reported on an automatic grenade launcher range which initiated during routine military training activities, according to an Oct. 22 statement from the Canadian Forces provost marshal. 41903273abf5b2735e0aa8ea7a65025f.text: Elections BC is set to begin finalizing the vote for the 2026 previncial election. Elections BC says it is set to begin counting roughly 150,000 absentee, mail-in and assisted telephone ballots not included in initial election-day counts. This will add significantly to the nearly 1.8 million ballots counted so far in the 2026 provincial election and could alter the result in several races. In Cowichan Valley, Conservative Bert Chen leads NDP’s Debra Toporowski by 151 votes. In Kelowna Centre, Conservative Kristina Loewen is ahead of the NDP’s Loyal Wooldridge by 132 votes. In Burnaby South-Metrotown, the NDP’s Paul Choi leads Conservative David Xie by 66 votes. NDP candidate Stephanie Higginson holds a razor-thin lead in Ladysmith-Oceanside. She leads Conservative Kris McNichol by just 13 votes. Those last two ridings are undergoing recounts, which are triggered when the margin is fewer than 100 votes. Five additional ridings have current margins of fewer than 500 votes, and seven more have margins of fewer than 1,000. Counting for the new batch of ballots will begin Friday, Nov. 6, and is expected to be completed on Nov. 10, when Elections BC will finalize results. These new ballots are sealed in certification envelopes to be checked before opening against votes cast on election day to prevent double voting. This marks the official end of vote-counting. The writs are to be returned on Nov. 18, allowing for members of the legislature to be sworn in. Conservative MLAs are scheduled to be sworn in on Nov. 19, Green Party MLAs on Nov. 23 and NDP MLAs on Nov. 26. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has not yet said whether the legislature will hold a short fall session.

A sample of some of the names, phrases and slogans written, inked or carved into the bridge in Centennial Park. One defining part of being human is wanting to be remembered. While that’s not quite universal, as plenty of people are content to go about their lives quietly, I would argue we all, on some level, want to be remembered by our friends and loved ones. We want to leave our mark on the world while we are here and after we, inevitably, are gone. I got to thinking about this recently while walking through Centennial Park, specifically across the bridge by Bridge Creek Falls. Along the wooden railings, you will often find graffiti, carved names and messages. Now, you might be inclined to dismiss such markings as vandalism and move on, but I stopped to think about the reasoning behind the messages written in pencil, marker or with the tip of a knife. On the one hand, it’s the action of bored individuals, but on the other, it is the continuation of a tradition as old as humanity. For millennia, we have sought to leave our mark on things that will outlast us. During the Stone Age, our ancestors would paint or carve scenes of everyday life into caves that either served as their homes or ritual spaces. Who these early artists were is long lost to us, yet their work remains. As agriculture was adopted and the first civilizations formed, this impulse to record our lives carried on. Egyptian Pharaohs recorded on their monuments and tombs the stories of their lives and those of their people. d779b61f11dcc58c7773de4821732ec4.text: Operation Red Nose Williams Lake is gearing up to provide safe rides home this holiday season. Volunteers will be at the ready this holiday season in Williams Lake to provide safe rides home. Operation Red Nose (ORN) is returning and will be available from 9 p.m. to 3 a.m. on Nov. 27, 28 and Dec. 4, 5, 11, 12, 18, 19 and 31. The service aimed at preventing impaired driving does not compete with taxi services, and instead provides people rides home within a 30-minute driving radius of Williams Lake in their own vehicles accompanied by a driver in a vehicle provided by local car dealerships. Rides are by donation, with all proceeds supporting local youth sports, including the the Williams Lake Minor Hockey Rep U18 Female and U18 Integrated teams, Cariboo Chilcotin Youth Fiddle Society, Cariboo Gymnastics Association and Cariboo Cheer All-Stars. The year’s program is being run by a team of Williams Lake Community Policing volunteers chaired by Donna Bergen, who has volunteered several years during ORN. “It’s coming along really good, so I feel pretty good,” Bergen said, adding she enjoys helping the community. “When you have people that you know that have died because of a drunk driver, you want to help people who are intoxicated get home.” According to a news release, outgoing ORN coordinator Deborah Pickering will continue to share her knowledge, as well as Dave Dickson, who was the first person to bring ORN to Williams Lake. ORN will once again be headquartered out of Heartland Toyota. “Year after year, support from the dealerships and party-goers who call for a ride ensure the program’s success, for which we are grateful,” the release stated. Bergen encourages anyone interested in volunteering with ORN to email her at donnabergen2022@gmail.com or call 250-267-9901. They’ll have to get a criminal record check. Each of the local youth sports receiving donation proceeds will also be supplying drivers.

aa416ee1136edc0ee1c53feb949fffc7.text: Environment Canada is warning of moderate to strong gusty winds across the Okanagan and much of B.C.’s Southern Interior later this afternoon (Saturday, Nov. 7) and continuing through Sunday evening. ​A special weather statement covers the Okanagan Connector, Coquihalla Highway, South Thompson, Nicola and other Interior regions. ​Southeasterly winds are expected to strengthen later Saturday, with gusts of 60 to 80 km/h across the Interior. Winds are forecast to peak by Sunday morning before easing. ​An incoming cold front is expected to push southwesterly winds into the region early Sunday afternoon, with gusts potentially reaching up to 90 km/h in western areas before calming down by Sunday night. ​Officials say local utility outages are possible and drivers should be prepared for crosswinds. Residents are advised to secure loose objects outdoors. ​The statement comes after a powerful coastal storm Friday that brought heavy rain and high winds to Vancouver Island. A separate rain warning remains in effect for the Fraser Canyon, where up to 50 mm of rain is expected through Sunday morning.

For a little over a decade, ending in 2019, Akhtar served as co-host for On the Island with Gregor Craigie. Over those years, he also created a food column the city is where Akhtar first began culinary teaching at Cook Culture (now gone from the iconic downtown Victoria building). He’d routinely teach classes on the principles of Indian cuisine, as a domestic cuisine, a backbone in his latest work, How to Eat with Your Hands. Norah Caldwell, co-author of the "Where is Lisa Marie Young?" book, was asked to help write the book by sister and Island Crime Podcast host Laura Palmer. The book "Where is Lisa Marie Young: The Disappearance of an Indigenous Woman and Her Family's Fight to Bring Her Home" has been released. Family and friends of an Indigenous woman who went missing in Nanaimo nearly 25 years ago, hope a new book sparks interest and possibly new leads in the investigation. _Where_ is _Lisa Marie Young: The Disappearance of an Indigenous Woman and Her Family’s Fight to Bring Her Home_ has been released by TouchWood Editions, delving into details about the woman whose last known whereabouts were in Nanaimo on June 30, 2002. It is co-authored by Carolann Bosma and Norah Caldwell and inspired by the Laura Palmer Island Crime Podcast. Speaking at a book reading at Nanaimo North Library Wednesday, Nov. 4, Bosma, Young’s foster sister, said penning the book was “definitely a journey emotionally, with lots of highs, lots of lows.” It was also an emotional process because there is still a lot of grief. Nanaimo RCMP have maintained constant communication, Bosma told the News Bulletin, and both hope the book is the catalyst for new leads. “That was one of the reasons why I agreed to write the book, is because we’re always looking for different ways to reach out to the community and our ultimate goal is to have Lisa come home,” said Bosma. “I’m really hoping the book is able to get into the hands of someone who possibly might have information and it’s almost like a quiet conversation with that person. 387edf7db8119896a27d31e348c9737a.text: BC Conservation Officer Service says officers will remain in close contact with the victims' families as well as the Nuxalk Nation and the community following a suspected fatal grizzly bear attack in Bella Coola. Testing is underway to determine if a captured grizzly bear in Bella Coola is linked to the recent attack that claimed the life of a mother and daughter. In a Friday, Nov. 6 Facebook post, BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) stated one grizzly bear has been captured. “In coordination with wildlife biologists and the provincial wildlife veterinarian from the Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship, the bear will be safely cared for while assessments are completed,” the post reads. Family has identified the victims as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 who failed to return after going for a walk on the Snooka West Trail. They were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack less than a year after several school children and one adult were left with serious injuries. A range of tools, including forensic DNA matching, distinctive physical measurements and other animal-specific characteristics, will be used by BCCOS to help determine if the captured bear is involved in the attacks. A team of Conservation Officers remain on the ground as trapping efforts continue. “Any bear confirmed to be responsible will be dispatched to protect public safety; unrelated bears will be released,” the Facebook post further stated. “Conservation Officers also have forensic and other evidence from the 2025 Bella Coola attack, which will be compared with evidence from any captured bears undergoing assessment.” The public is urged to continue avoiding the West Snooka Trail area where several bear sightings near the area of the fatal attacks have been reported. “This is a devastating and deeply unfortunate event that has had a profound impact on the families, the Nuxalk Nation, and the broader Bella Coola community. e15bc3c56316c51afb69d61e59937e63.text: A pickup truck driver was taken to the hospital following a collision involving two tractor-trailers on Highway 97 north of Prince George. In a press release, Prince George RCMP said it is investigating the collision, which occurred on Monday, Nov. 2, north of Bear Lake, approximately 70 kilometres north of Prince George. The multi-vehicle collision involved two tractor-trailers and a pickup truck. According to the release, emergency responders attended the scene after receiving reports of the incident. The pickup truck driver sustained injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening. Mounties said the cause of the collision has not yet been determined, and the investigation remains in its early stages. Highway 97 north of Bear Lake is currently open to alternating single-lane traffic. Motorists are encouraged to check DriveBC for the latest road conditions, traffic advisories and closure information before travelling through the area.
